steps.body: Two classes record hours of weekly reading. **Class A:** 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10. **Class B:** 1, 2, 6, 8, 12, 13. Both sum to 42, so both means are 42 ÷ 6 = **7** — and both medians are (6 + 8) ÷ 2 = **7** too. Every center agrees the classes match. But look at the plots: A hugs its center; B scatters. Centers alone can hide the whole story.
Draw the center and spread together.

widget.prompt: Class B is 1, 2, 6, 8, 12, 13. Set its five-number summary. Put the median halfway between the middle values 6 and 8.
widget.successFeedback: The median is 7, halfway between 6 and 8. The wide box from Q1 = 2 to Q3 = 12 also makes Class B's larger spread visible.
widget.orderFeedback: Keep the five markers in order: minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum.
widget.valueFeedback: Use the sorted data and the halves of three: minimum 1, Q1 2, median 7, Q3 12, maximum 13.

predict.prompt: This data set has SIX values. Will its median be one of the listed numbers, or sit between two of them?

options.label: Always one of the listed numbers
It's the biggest minus the smallest

predict.reveal: An even count has no single middle value — the median splits the difference between the two central numbers.

explanationVariants: Class B splits into halves 1, 2, 6 and 8, 12, 13, so Q1 = 2 and Q3 = 12: IQR = 12 − 2 = 10 — against Class A's IQR of just 4.
Each half's middle value is its quartile: 2 below, 12 above. The middle half of Class B is 10 wide, more than double Class A's.

widget.prompt: Class A's IQR is 4. Compute Class B's IQR (data 1, 2, 6, 8, 12, 13 — halves of three).

commonErrors.feedback: 4 is Class A's IQR — the point is that B differs! B's halves 1, 2, 6 and 8, 12, 13 give Q1 = 2 and Q3 = 12: IQR = 10.
14 adds the quartiles (12 + 2). The IQR is their difference: 12 − 2 = 10.

hints: Split B's six values into two halves of three.

steps.body: Spread is what those numbers mean **in context**. Class A (IQR 4): most students read a similar amount — a 7-hour-ish plan suits nearly everyone. Class B (IQR 10): the 'typical 7 hours' describes almost nobody; some students read barely at all while others devour books. Same center, opposite classrooms. A center without a spread is **half a description**.

widget.prompt: Drag each summary to the question it answers.

buckets.label: SPREAD — how far do values scatter?

items.label: Mean
items.feedback: The mean is a level-out value — it locates the data's balance point, a center.

items.label: Median
items.feedback: The median is the middle of the sorted line-up — a center, not a stretch.

items.label: Range
items.feedback: Max − min measures how far the data STRETCHES — that's spread.

items.label: IQR
items.feedback: The width of the middle half is a scatter measure — spread, the outlier-resistant kind.

widget.missFeedback: Ask what the number tells you: a LOCATION on the number line (center) or a WIDTH along it (spread)?
widget.successFeedback: Two centers, two spreads — a full description borrows one of each.

explanationVariants: Consistency is small spread. Class A's IQR of 4 means its middle half sits within a narrow 4-hour band — those students read similar amounts.
The tighter the middle half, the more alike the students: IQR 4 beats IQR 10 for consistency.

widget.prompt: A librarian wants the class whose students read the MOST SIMILAR amounts. Class A: center 7, IQR 4. Class B: center 7, IQR 10. Which class — and on what evidence?

options.label: Class A — its smaller IQR means the middle half bunches tightly
options.feedback: Right — similarity is a SPREAD question, and A's middle half spans only 4 hours.

options.label: They're identical — both centers are 7
options.feedback: The centers match, but centers can't see scatter: B's students range from 1 to 13 hours. The IQRs (4 vs 10) break the tie.

options.label: Class B — a bigger IQR means more data in the middle
options.feedback: Both middle halves hold the same FRACTION of students; the IQR measures how WIDE that half is. Wider (10) means more scattered, not more central.

hints: Is 'most similar' a center question or a spread question?

steps.body: Match the numbers to the plots.
explanationVariants: Range checks: A stretches 4 to 10 (range 6); B stretches 1 to 13 (range 12) — the scattered plot owns the bigger stretch.
Every spread measure agrees here: B doubles A on range (12 vs 6) just as it did on IQR (10 vs 4).

widget.prompt: One more spread measure: what is Class B's RANGE (data 1, 2, 6, 8, 12, 13)?

commonErrors.feedback: 6 is Class A's range (10 − 4). Class B stretches wider: 13 − 1 = 12.
14 adds max and min (13 + 1). Range subtracts them: 13 − 1 = 12.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Max 13, min 1: range = 13 − 1 = 12 — double Class A's 6, matching the IQR story.

explanationVariants: Only (a) pairs a center (median 7) with a spread (IQR 10) — the two-part summary this chapter has been building toward.
'Center 7, spread 10' answers both questions: where the data sits AND how far it scatters.

widget.prompt: Which report FULLY describes Class B's reading hours with two numbers?

options.label: "Median 7 hours, IQR 10 hours" — a center plus a spread
options.feedback: That's the complete pair — location and scatter together. Anyone reading it knows B is centered like A but far more varied.

options.label: "Mean 7 and median 7" — two summaries must be enough
options.feedback: That's two CENTERS — the same question answered twice. Class A posts identical numbers, so this report can't tell the classes apart. Pair a center with a spread.

options.label: "Range 12 and IQR 10" — spread is the interesting part
options.feedback: Two SPREADS with no location — how much scatter, but around what? Swap one for a center: median 7 plus IQR 10 tells the whole story.

hints: A full description answers two different questions.
Where is the middle? How wide is the scatter?

takeaways: Data sets can share every center yet differ wildly: A and B both had mean AND median 7.
Spread broke the tie — IQR 4 vs 10, range 6 vs 12.
A full two-number description pairs one center with one spread.
steps.teaser: next: turning the five-number summary into a picture — the box plot — and then a second way to measure spread.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **Centers locate, spreads scatter.** The sets 6, 7, 8 and 1, 7, 13 both have median 7 — but the first spans a range of 2 while the second spans 12. Spread is what tells them apart.

explanationVariants: Range = 13 − 1 = 12; the other set's range is only 8 − 6 = 2.
Same middle, six times the stretch: 12 versus 2.

widget.prompt: The sets 6, 7, 8 and 1, 7, 13 both have median 7. What is the RANGE of 1, 7, 13?

commonErrors.feedback: 2 is the range of the OTHER set (8 − 6). This one stretches 13 − 1 = 12.
7 is the shared median — a center. The range is max − min: 13 − 1 = 12.
